steps: Wheel is to bicycle as page is to book.
An analogy compares two relationships. Name the connection in the first pair, then apply it to the second pair in the same order.
A wheel is part of a bicycle. A page is part of a book. Both pairs go from a part to its whole.
Paper is related to page, but paper is the material a page is made from.
Match the relationship and its direction.
A documentary and a public service announcement can both discuss the environment. They do different jobs.

A viewing genre is a type of program. Look at its purpose, intended audience, and format. A documentary explores real events or issues. A public service announcement asks viewers to take an action. A trailer previews a film.
A short video shows families reducing waste and ends with “Bring a reusable bag.” The request is evidence that the clip aims to persuade viewers to act.
A platform tells you where the video appears. The same platform can show news, a trailer, an educational program, or animation.
Identify the genre by what the video does and how it does it.
The club painted the sign. The sign was painted by the club.
In active voice, the subject does the action. In passive voice, the subject receives the action, and the verb uses a form of be plus the past participle.
Move the sign into subject position. Use was painted to keep the past tense.
The sign is painted changes the tense.
Change the focus and keep the action and tense.

g7-q1-m4.topic: How to describe a finished action
steps: Yesterday, Ana packed lunch and went to school.
Use simple past for finished past events. Regular verbs usually take -ed. Irregular verbs have their own forms.
Pack becomes packed. Go becomes went. The word yesterday tells when the actions happened.
Avoid goed. With did, use the base form in Did Ana go?
Find the past time, then choose the right verb form.
At 7:10 the bus left. At 7:15 Mia arrived.
Use had plus the past participle to mark an action already finished before another point in the past. A past participle is the verb form used after had, such as left or finished.
The bus had left before Mia arrived. Had left marks the 7:10 event. Arrived gives the later past event.
Had went is incorrect. Go changes to gone after had.
Past perfect looks back from a point in the past.
Sam said, “I am tired.” Later, Lia reported his words.
Direct speech gives the speaker’s exact words. Reported speech retells the message and may adjust pronouns, time words and tense to fit the new viewpoint.
Lia says, “Sam said that he was tired.” I becomes he because Sam is the person being described.
Sam said that I was tired would refer to the person reporting the words.
Keep the meaning while changing the viewpoint.

g7-q1-m7.topic: Phrases and their jobs in a sentence
steps: Compare after the game and after the game ended.
A phrase is a group of words that acts as a unit. Unlike a clause, it has no subject and verb working together.
After the game tells when and has no verb. After the game ended has the subject game and the verb ended.
Several words together do not automatically make a clause.
Check for a subject and its verb.
Because the bus stopped leaves a thought unfinished.
A clause contains a subject and a verb. An independent clause can stand alone. A dependent clause needs another clause to complete the thought.
Because the bus stopped, we walked. Bus stopped belongs to the reason clause; we walked can stand alone.
A capital letter and period cannot complete a dependent clause.
Pair dependent clauses with a complete thought.
The bell rang. The bell rang, and the doors opened.

Sentence structure depends on the kinds and number of clauses. A simple sentence has one independent clause. A compound sentence joins two. A complex sentence joins a dependent clause to an independent one.
When the bell rang, the doors opened is complex. The when-clause depends on the rest.
A sentence with and can still be simple if and joins two words instead of two clauses.
Count clauses by checking for subject–verb units.
A timetable and a news story need different kinds of reading.
Skim to get the main idea, scan for a specific detail, and read closely when meaning depends on exact wording.
Scan the route column for Route 4 and read across to find 8:20. Skim the headings of a news story to tell what it covers.
Reading every line is inefficient when you only need one time.
Let your purpose choose the reading style.

g7-q2-m1.topic: Listening for the information you need
steps: A crowded station announcement gives a gate change.
Before listening, decide what you need to hear and recall what you know. During listening, use clues and check details you missed.
If you need your gate, listen for your route and the gate number. Then replay or ask for that part again.
Writing every word can make you miss the detail you need.
Listen for information that serves your purpose.
A search for jaguar returns both animals and cars.
A search engine finds pages using your search words. Specific terms narrow the results.
Try jaguar habitat to focus on the animal. Read the result title and snippet before opening it.
The top result may be an ad or may answer a different question.
Choose precise keywords and inspect results.
A route notice, a classmate and a blog disagree about a bus schedule.
An information source can be a person, publication or digital resource. Choose a source that fits the question and check who provided it and when.
For today’s departure, compare the date on the operator’s notice with the date on the blog.
A printed document can be out of date even when it looks official.
Match the source to the question and date.
One paragraph explains why a shop changed its hours.

A summary gives the main points briefly. A précis is a concise restatement that preserves the original argument or order. A paraphrase restates a specific idea in your own words at a similar level of detail.
Original idea: The shop opens later on Fridays so staff can count stock. Paraphrase: Friday opening is delayed while staff check inventory. Short summary: Stock checks affect Friday hours.
Changing a few words while copying the sentence structure is weak paraphrasing.
Preserve the meaning while changing the length or wording to fit the task.
A paragraph lists when three clubs meet.
Linear text follows a reading sequence. Nonlinear text lets readers enter through a heading, row, branch or label.
Put Chess, Drama and Art in separate rows with day and room columns. To find Drama’s room, read across that row.
A misplaced room number changes the information.
Change the format and preserve the facts.

g7-q3-m1.topic: Choosing media that clarify a speech
steps: A slide shows where runners turn while the speaker explains the route.
Multimedia combines resources such as text, images, audio or video. Each resource should help the audience understand the spoken message.
Use a map for the turn and say, “Turn left after the bridge.” Both cues point to the same spot.
A busy photo can distract listeners from the direction they need.
Choose media for a specific job.
The same announcement can be read or delivered from brief notes.
Manuscript delivery reads a script. Memorized delivery recalls it word for word. Impromptu delivery has little preparation. Extemporaneous delivery uses preparation and notes with flexible wording.
For a precise emergency notice, read the script. For a prepared club report, use a few cue cards and explain naturally.
Speaking from notes is different from speaking with no preparation.
Match the delivery method to the situation.
In the Maranao folk epic The Good Prince Bantugan, the people praise Bantugan for his courage and goodness.
A folk epic is a long traditional story about a hero. A character’s strength is a quality that can be inferred from what they do and how others respond.
When enemies attack Bumbaran, Bantugan leads soldiers to defend it. That action supports an inference of courage. The praise he receives shows how others see him.
An inference needs evidence. Calling a character brave without pointing to an action only repeats the label.
Name the strength and connect it to a specific action in the story.

g7-q3-m4.topic: Supporting a belief about something you viewed
steps: Two viewers react differently to a poster about wasting food.
A belief is a view you hold. A conviction is a firmly held belief. Explain yours with a specific detail from the material.
“I believe taking smaller portions could help because the poster shows unfinished food on several plates.” The visible detail supports the response.
“Everyone wastes food” goes beyond what the poster shows.
State your belief and connect it to a viewed detail.

g7-q3-m5.topic: Matching evidence to a general statement
steps: “The canteen was busy” needs evidence.
Evidence is a specific detail that supports a general statement. Choose a detail that actually bears on the claim.
“The line reached the door at noon” supports the claim about crowding. The price of a sandwich does not.
A detail from the same place may still be irrelevant.
Ask how the detail helps show the claim is true.
“The match ended 2–1” and “It was the best match” do different jobs.
A fact can be checked against evidence. An opinion expresses a judgment or preference.
Check the score against the match record. Ask the speaker what made the match best for them.
A strongly stated opinion is still a judgment.
Ask whether evidence can verify the statement as written.
A message says a club meeting has moved.
Wh-questions ask for specific information. Who asks about people, where asks about place, when asks about time, why asks about reasons and how asks about manner.
“Where did the club meet?” asks for a place and uses did plus meet. “Who moved the meeting?” asks for the subject and needs no did.
“When did the club met?” incorrectly repeats the past form.
Pick the question word for the detail you need.
“The results were pretty good” is vague in a report.
Academic writing uses precise, organized language and supports statements with evidence. The tone suits a reader who needs to check the claim.
“Twelve of the fifteen seedlings grew” states the result more clearly and gives a count.
Formal vocabulary alone cannot make an unsupported claim reliable.
Use exact words and show the evidence.
A student asks a librarian about a missing book.
An interview gathers information through planned questions. Conversation and dialogue also rely on listening, turn-taking and clarification.
Ask, “When was the book last checked in?” Follow with, “Which shelf should I check?”
Interrupting with a different question can lose a useful detail.
Listen to the reply before asking the next question.

g7-q4-m3.topic: Which ideas matter to the main point?
steps: A talk about school transport mentions delays and the speaker’s favorite color.
Judge an idea by its relevance to the topic and how well it is supported.
A week of delay records helps explain a transport problem. A color preference contributes little to that question.
A memorable remark may carry little weight.
Ask what each idea contributes to the speaker’s point.

g7-q4-m4.topic: Checking what a viewed claim actually shows
steps: A video caption says a recent flood closed a road.
Check a viewed claim by comparing its date, place and details with reliable independent sources.
Look for an official road notice for the named place and date. A real flood video from another year cannot establish today’s closure.
A familiar logo or dramatic image is weak proof by itself.
Verify the claim and the context of its evidence.
Two characters want the same practice room.
Conflict is a struggle between opposing needs, forces or choices. A peaceful resolution addresses those needs without harm.
The groups explain why they need the room and agree on two time slots. Both can rehearse.
Ending the argument by silencing one group leaves its problem unresolved.
Identify the conflict, then examine how the solution responds to it.

g7-q4-m6.topic: Identity and perspective in a legend
steps: The Legend of Mayon Volcano connects a well-known landscape in Albay with the story of Daragang Magayon.
A legend is a traditional story often connected to a place or person. To understand a character’s identity, look at what the story calls them, the choices they make, and the community around them.
The text introduces Daragang Magayon in Rawis and explains the meaning of her name. Reading that detail alongside the Bicol setting helps explain why the name matters in this story.
A detail from a legend can explain a cultural story or belief. It does not serve as a scientific explanation of the landscape.
Connect a detail about the character to the story’s setting and cultural context.

g7-q4-m7.topic: Cooperation and responsibility in a story
steps: A short story can show how people share a responsibility through the choices its characters make.

The setting is where and when the story happens. Characters are the people in it. The plot is the sequence of events, and the conflict is the problem the characters face. A theme is a larger idea the story develops through those elements.

After a storm, one neighbor checks who needs supplies while another organizes deliveries. The storm creates the problem, and each character’s action helps solve it. Together, those actions develop a theme about sharing responsibility.
Merely being present does not show what a character contributed. Point to an action and explain how it affects what happens next.
Connect a character’s choice and its consequences to the theme of the story.
A reader wants to know how to care for a borrowed book.
An informative essay explains a topic using a clear introduction, organized details and a conclusion.
Introduce book care, group details by storage and handling, then recap the most useful steps.
Adding an unrelated opinion can interrupt the explanation.
Organize facts around one clear purpose.
“The path was slick, so the runners slowed to avoid slipping.”
Context clues are words or ideas nearby that help you infer a word’s meaning.
Slipping and slowed point to slick meaning slippery. Try replacing slick with slippery and reread the sentence.
A nearby word can be unrelated. Check the meaning against the whole sentence.
Test a guessed meaning in context.

g8-q1-m2.topic: Collecting details for a Chicago bibliography
steps: A journal article and an online newspaper story may both help your research. A reader needs enough information to find each one.

A bibliography lists the sources used in a work. This module uses Chicago’s notes and bibliography style, 17th edition. Start by identifying the source type, then collect the relevant details, such as author, title, publication, date, and pages or URL.

In the lesson’s printed-journal example, Juana Martinez is the author, “Distance Learning Amidst COVID-19” is the article, and Journal of Studies in Philippine Education is the journal. Put those details in the matching places in a journal entry.
Do not swap the article title and journal title or apply the book format to every source. Use the conventions for that type of source.
Identify the source type, collect its details, then follow the matching bibliography format.
“It might rain” and “There is a possibility of rain” signal possibility.
Modals express meanings such as possibility, certainty or obligation. A modal verb helps a main verb, a modal noun names the idea and a modal adverb modifies the strength of a statement.
Compare “It might rain,” “There is a possibility of rain” and “It will probably rain.” Their forms differ, and all leave uncertainty.
Use might rain, without to after might.
Choose the form and strength that fit your meaning.
“The room was full. Therefore, we waited outside.”
Transition signals show relations between ideas, such as result, contrast, addition or sequence.
Therefore points to a result. However would set up a contrast, as in “The room was full. However, the meeting started on time.”
A polished transition can still show the wrong relationship.
Name the relationship before selecting the signal.

g8-q1-m5.topic: Using words to express a response and persuade
steps: A notice asks students to save water.
Verbs, adjectives and adverbs can show an emotional response and strengthen a persuasive appeal.
“I urge our class to repair the wasteful tap promptly.” Urge expresses the appeal, wasteful gives a judgment and promptly sets urgency.
Strong words without a reason may sound forceful but leave the case weak.
Use expressive words to support a clear reason.

g8-q2-m1.topic: Connecting a visual to its caption
steps: A bar chart shows 12 library loans on Monday, 18 on Tuesday and 15 on Wednesday.
A visual–verbal relationship connects what a visual shows with what words explain. Check the title, labels, unit and values before writing a caption.
“Tuesday had the most loans of the three days” is supported by 18, compared with 12 and 15. “Tuesday is always busiest” goes beyond the dates shown.
Do not confuse loans with borrowers or three days with a usual pattern.
Say exactly what the visual supports.

g8-q2-m2.topic: Signaling an opinion and giving a reason
steps: “The gym opens at 8” and “In my view, 8 is too late” make different claims.
An opinion-marking signal introduces a view or judgment. Examples include in my view and I believe.
“In my view, the gym should open earlier” states a preference. A reason, such as morning practice, explains it.
An opinion marker does not turn an unverified claim into a fact.
Mark your opinion and give the reason for it.

g8-q2-m3.topic: Comparing how words, pictures, and sound inform
steps: A poster and an audio announcement describe the same event.
Multimodal texts combine ways of communicating, such as images, print and sound. Compare the information and how each format emphasizes it.
Both give the event date. The poster makes the location easy to revisit; the announcement uses repetition to help listeners catch it.
Different formats do not always give different facts.
Compare shared content and the effect of each mode.
Two students agree on a reading break but prefer different times.
To compare opinions, state each view fairly, identify common ground and explain the difference with reasons.
“We both support a reading break. I prefer morning because the room is quiet, while Ben prefers afternoon because more students can attend.”
Disagreeing with timing does not mean disagreeing with the goal.
Separate agreement, disagreement and reasons.
A review says, “The wait was frustrating,” then adds, “Just what I needed: another hour in line.”
Literal language states its message directly. Figurative language can suggest a positive or negative attitude through context, comparison or irony.
“Frustrating” states a negative response. “Just what I needed” sounds positive on its own, but “another hour in line” suggests a complaint in this context.
A positive-sounding phrase can convey criticism. Read the surrounding words before judging the tone.
Use wording and context to explain the message and its attitude.

g8-q3-m1.topic: Recognizing bias in wording and selection
steps: A report calls one plan “brilliant” and the other “ridiculous.”
Bias is a leaning that can affect how a text selects or presents information.
Compare the report with a version that describes both plans’ costs and benefits. Loaded adjectives reveal the writer’s slant.
A text may show bias by leaving out information even when it uses calm language.
Check wording and whose evidence is included.

g8-q3-m2.topic: Identifying techniques that influence an audience
steps: A poster says “Everyone has this backpack.”
Propaganda uses techniques to influence beliefs or behavior. Bandwagon appeals to the desire to join others; a testimonial uses an endorsement.
“Everyone has this backpack” is bandwagon. “A sports star recommends it” uses a testimonial.
Popularity alone says little about durability.
Name the technique and inspect the evidence behind it.

g8-q3-m3.topic: Distinguishing social, moral, and economic issues
steps: A speaker describes crowded housing, an unfair rule and rising rent.
A social issue affects how people live together. A moral issue involves judgments about right and wrong. An economic issue concerns resources, money or livelihood.
Rising rent raises an economic issue. An unfair rule raises a moral concern. The same situation can involve several categories.
Avoid classifying an issue from one keyword alone.
Listen for what the speaker says is at stake.

g8-q3-m4.topic: Reading stories in their cultural context
steps: In The Story of the Aged Mother, a son faces an unjust order, and his mother’s wisdom later helps the community.
Heritage includes stories, customs, and values passed between generations. Look at choices and consequences in a story to see how a value is expressed.

The mother helps solve the problem of making a rope of ashes. Her role supports a reading about the value of older people’s knowledge. Compare how the ruler treats older people before their knowledge is needed.
One story does not speak for every member of a culture. Keep the interpretation tied to the characters and details in the selection.
Use a specific story detail to explain a value in its cultural context.
“Lina borrowed a novel. She returned it on Friday.”
Cohesive devices connect sentences. Pronouns refer back to earlier words and conjunctions show relations between ideas.
She points to Lina and it points to the novel. The links let the reader follow the topic without repetition.
A pronoun with two plausible referents can confuse readers.
Make every connection easy to follow.

g8-q3-m6.topic: Matching grammatical patterns in a series
steps: “The club enjoys reading, drawing and to sing” sounds uneven.
Parallel structure uses the same grammatical pattern for ideas of equal importance.
Revise to “reading, drawing and singing.” All three items now use the same verb form.
Repeating a word does not fix a mismatch in grammatical form.
Read the items as a set and match their forms.
A school notice can start with a broad claim, explain a cause, or respond to an opposing idea.

Idea development is the way a writer organizes a point. The module uses general to particular, cause and effect, claim and counterclaim, problem and solution, and persuasion. Signals tell readers how ideas fit together.
In an original notice, “Because the line blocks the doorway” gives a cause. “One way to solve this is to move the queue outside” introduces a solution. Each phrase signals a different relationship.
A transition is useful only when it matches the relationship. “As a result” should introduce a result the earlier sentence actually supports.
Choose the organizing pattern first, then the words that make the relationship clear.
An outline about library use has a heading but few details.
A primary source supplies direct evidence. A secondary source interprets or summarizes evidence. Notes from both can support different outline points.
Put the library’s daily loan record under use patterns and a report interpreting several libraries’ records under comparison.
Collecting notes without assigning them to points can leave the outline unfocused.
Place each source note where it supports an idea.
Two notices give different details about a reading event.
Synthesis combines relevant ideas from several sources into a new explanation.
One notice gives the date and another gives the entry requirements. Combine them into a single accurate event description and identify where each detail came from.
Listing source summaries one after another leaves the connections for the reader.
Connect the sources around one question.
A paragraph about a canteen line mentions unrelated homework.
An effective paragraph develops one controlling idea with relevant details in a clear order.
“The canteen line moves faster with two counters.” Follow with details about orders and payment that explain why.
A detail can be interesting and still distract from the main point.
Make every detail support the paragraph’s main idea.
A description of a queue and an explanation of how to join it serve different purposes.
Text types organize paragraphs according to purpose, such as describing, recounting, explaining or giving steps.
A description shows where the queue bends. A procedural paragraph gives numbered actions for joining the line.
A list of qualities cannot substitute for steps when the reader needs instructions.
Let the purpose guide the paragraph’s structure.

g8-q4-m6.topic: Writing and delivering a clear speech
steps: A speech about a reading club sounds different when delivered aloud.
Plan a speech around its audience, purpose and topic. Use clear articulation, pacing, emphasis and suitable body language.
Pause after “Our club needs one quiet hour,” then emphasize “one” so the request is easy to hear.
Reading every line at the same speed makes key ideas harder to identify.
Plan the message and rehearse the delivery.
A lab notice says you may enter, must wear goggles and must not eat.
Modal verbs help express permission, obligation and prohibition. Permission allows an action, obligation requires one and prohibition forbids it.
“You must wear goggles” requires goggles. “You must not eat” forbids eating. “You don’t have to bring gloves” removes a requirement.
Must not and do not have to have different meanings.
Choose the modal that matches the rule’s force.
“If the screen gets wet, the touch controls often stop responding.”
The zero conditional describes a general result. Use a present form in the condition and the result when stating a general pattern.
“If you press Save, the editor stores your changes.” The sentence describes how the editor works each time.
An expected result of one future event belongs in a different pattern.
Use zero conditional for rules and repeated results.
The match is tomorrow and rain is possible.
The first conditional connects a real future possibility to its likely or planned result. A common pattern is if plus simple present, then will plus base verb.
“If it rains tomorrow, we will move practice indoors.” The rain is possible and the move depends on it.
In this pattern, use if it rains, rather than if it will rain.
Use the first conditional for a possible future and its consequence.

g9-q1-w4.topic: Imagining a different present or future
steps: A class has one laptop but imagines having five.
The second conditional imagines an unlikely or unreal present or future situation. Use if plus past form and would plus base verb in a common pattern.
“If we had five laptops, each group would have one.” Had marks the imagined situation here.
The past form here does not make the situation a past event.
Second conditional asks what would happen in a different situation.
Mia submitted the file after the deadline. Imagine she had submitted it earlier.

A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. In the third conditional, the if-clause imagines a different past using had plus past participle. The result clause uses would, could or might have plus past participle.
“If Mia had submitted the file before noon, it would have arrived on time.” Had submitted imagines a different action. Would have arrived shows the imagined result.
“If Mia would have submitted” puts the result form in the if-clause. Use if Mia had submitted.
The past stays the same. The sentence imagines what could have changed.

g9-q1-w6.topic: Choosing among the four conditional patterns
steps: Four messages use if to describe a rule, a plan, a wish and a regret.
Zero covers a general pattern. First covers a real future possibility. Second imagines a different present or future. Third imagines a different past.
Compare “If it rains, the yard gets wet,” “If it rains tomorrow, we’ll play indoors,” “If we had a gym, we’d play inside” and “If we had booked a room, we would have played.”
Do not pick a form by looking at if alone.
Decide when the situation happens and how real it is.
At a ceremony, the audience recites an established pledge. Later, an organizer welcomes families using their own words.

Communicative style is the way someone uses language for a particular situation. Frozen style uses established wording. The conversational style discussed in this module uses natural, familiar wording to engage listeners.
In an original example, a school recites its pledge word for word. Then the host says, “Welcome, families. Let me show you where to sit.” The pledge is fixed; the welcome sounds conversational.
Do not assume that every message spoken at a ceremony has fixed wording. Check the job each message does.
Look at who is listening, why you are speaking, and whether the words are fixed.
You ask a teacher for help, message a friend, and speak privately with someone close to you. Each setting calls for different wording.

Consultative style gives information and invites feedback, as in a teacher–student conversation. Casual style uses informal language between familiar people. Intimate style relies on shared understanding between people who are very close.

In an original example, a student asks a teacher, “Could you show me the next step?” A friend texts, “See you after practice.” A sibling says, “The usual?” and a shared routine supplies the missing detail.
Casual and intimate styles can both sound informal. Intimate speech can depend on private context that an outsider would miss.
Choose a style that fits how well the speakers know each other and what they need to communicate.

g9-q2-m1.topic: Connecting a text detail to a real issue
steps: A story shows a student missing meetings because there is no late bus.
A text-to-world connection links a specific detail to a real issue and explains the relationship.
The missed meetings suggest a transport barrier. Check local transport data before claiming how widespread it is.
A personal association needs a clear link to the text.
Move from detail to issue to a reasoned connection.

g9-q2-m2.topic: How language shapes a reader’s view of the world
steps: A speech can show what a community is facing and what the speaker hopes will change.
Look at the author’s purpose and how word choices support it. Tone is the speaker’s attitude. Mood is the feeling the language creates for the audience. Repetition can make a key idea stand out.

In Martin Luther King Jr.’s speech, the repeated phrase “I have a dream” introduces different hopes for racial equality. The repetition connects those hopes and helps listeners picture the future King is asking them to work toward.
Keep tone and mood separate. A speaker can sound determined while making listeners feel hopeful.
Use a specific language choice and its context to explain what the speech helps readers understand.
A report favors one team. A spectator judges a player by their background before seeing them play.
Bias is a leaning that affects judgment. Prejudice is a judgment formed in advance, often about a person or group without fair evidence.
Choosing only favorable scores suggests bias. Assuming a new player cannot play because of their background shows prejudice.
A fair criticism of a specific action is different from judging a whole group.
Ask what shaped the judgment and what evidence was used.
A video about recycling includes a clear collection schedule and an unrelated sports clip.
Relevance asks whether an idea bears on the topic. Truthfulness asks whether reliable evidence supports it.
The schedule is relevant. Compare it with the collector’s dated notice to check if it is true.
Relevant information can still be false.
Check usefulness and accuracy separately.

g9-q3-w3.topic: Checking the context behind a clip
steps: A clip says the school will close early and shows an undated photo.
Test whether a viewed detail proves the exact claim being made.
An official notice for today would help confirm the early closing. An undated photo may show a real closure at another time.
A real image can be used in a misleading context.
Verify the time, place and source of the evidence.
Two clips make different claims about the same project.
Compare the wording, evidence and sources before deciding which claims are relevant and trustworthy.
One clip names a recent inspection and the other gives an anonymous rumor. Look up the inspection to check what it actually says.
Repeated claims may come from one original rumor.
Corroborate with independent evidence.

g9-q3-w6.topic: How much can a piece of evidence prove?
steps: A speaker supports a proposal with a single story from a friend.
Validity concerns whether evidence gives a sound basis for the claim. Check relevance, accuracy and how much the evidence can establish.
One student’s trip shows that a delay happened once. A dated series of trip records is stronger support for a claim about frequent delays.
One vivid example cannot establish a common pattern.
Match the strength of your conclusion to the evidence.

g9-q3-w7.topic: Finding the speaker’s claim and evidence
steps: A speech claims an extra study room would help and mentions a sign-in count.
Separate the speaker’s claim from examples, testimony and data offered as evidence.
“Ten students were turned away on Tuesday” is a data claim. Ask who counted, when and whether the number supports the wider proposal.
Confidence in delivery cannot verify a number.
Identify the evidence before deciding how much it proves.
A speaker claims a change helped all students based on one club’s survey.
Evaluate whether evidence is relevant, trustworthy and representative. Representative evidence reflects the wider group being discussed.
A chess-club survey may show what that club thinks. It cannot by itself tell what all students think.
A large percentage can still come from a narrow sample.
Check who the evidence represents before generalizing.

g9-q4-m1.topic: Showing the strength of an evaluation
steps: A review says a repair might help, then says it is essential.
Evaluation expresses a judgment and the strength of that judgment. Modals and evaluative words help readers see possibility, recommendation or necessity.
“The repair could reduce leaks” expresses possibility. “It is essential to replace the cracked pipe” gives a stronger judgment that needs evidence.
Do not use a strong modal to make weak evidence seem certain.
Match evaluative language to the strength of the evidence.

g9-q4-m2.topic: Relating a text to a real concern
steps: A story’s character cannot study at home because the shared room is noisy.
Connect the text to a real concern by explaining the similarity and its limits.
The detail relates to access to quiet study space. A school survey could help tell whether classmates experience a similar problem.
Sharing one detail does not make two situations identical.
Explain where the text and the real issue connect.
A lost key matters because it prevents a character from entering before dark.
Plot is the sequence of events. Setting is the time and place. Conflict is the struggle. Theme is a larger idea developed by the story.
A locked door at night raises the stakes. The character’s choice to ask for help can contribute to a theme about trust if other events support it.
Theme is more than a one-word topic.
Explain how story elements work together.
An article claims a longer lunch would improve attendance.
Judge relevance, reasoning and presentation separately. Reasoning explains how evidence supports a conclusion.
Attendance records show when students are absent. They do not show a lunch schedule caused the absences without further evidence.
A neat chart cannot repair a weak link between evidence and conclusion.
Check the argument even when the presentation looks convincing.

g9-q4-m5.topic: Weighing evidence and deciding what matters
steps: A speaker calls for a temporary path closure after reporting a damaged rail.
A value judgment weighs what ought to matter, such as safety, fairness or urgency. Identify evidence and consider the effects of an action.
An inspection report supports the safety concern. A temporary closure and alternate route respond to both safety and access.
An emotional appeal alone cannot establish urgency.
Explain which values and evidence support your judgment.

g9-q4-m6.topic: Making a prediction from what you hear
steps: A recorded announcement says the creek has risen after hours of rain.
A prediction says what may happen next. A projection extends a known trend under stated assumptions.
“If heavy rain continues, the creek may rise further” connects the forecast to a condition. A pause in rain could change the outcome.
Do not state a prediction as a certainty.
State the evidence, assumption and possible outcome.
A reviewer favors a friend’s entry and dismisses another entrant based on a stereotype.
Bias can favor or disfavor someone. Prejudice makes an advance judgment about a person or group without sufficient evidence.
Giving a friend extra credit shows favoritism. Assuming a newcomer lacks skill without seeing their work shows prejudice.
Disagreement based on clear criteria is not automatically prejudice.
Identify the unfair influence and check the evidence.
Three practice sessions ran late after setup problems.
A generalization draws a broader conclusion from examples. Its scope should reflect the size and range of the evidence.
“Setup delays affected these three sessions” fits the records. “Practice always starts late” needs broader evidence.
Words like all and always can overstate a pattern.
Make the conclusion only as broad as the evidence allows.

g9-q4-m9.topic: Comparing the scope of a claim and its proof
steps: A clip shows a tidy classroom and claims every room is ready.
A viewed claim is relevant when it addresses the issue and trustworthy when the evidence supports its scope.
A clip of one room supports a claim about that room. A dated checklist for all rooms would better support the wider claim.
One image cannot establish what happened outside its frame.
Compare the scope of the claim with the scope of the evidence.

g9-q4-m11.topic: How a play develops a theme
steps: A character repeats a promise in two scenes but breaks it in the last act.
A play develops theme through dialogue, actions, stage directions and the sequence of scenes and acts.
The repeated promise and later action can build a theme about trust. Use both scenes to explain the contrast.
One memorable line may be too little evidence for the whole play’s theme.
Trace how choices across scenes build a larger idea.
An actor says “Come in” while stepping back and opening the door.
Verbal communication uses words and vocal delivery. Nonverbal communication includes gesture, posture, movement and facial expression.
A quiet invitation and an open gesture support welcome. The same words and a raised hand can suggest hesitation.
Big gestures can distract if they do not suit the character or scene.
Make the words and actions support the intended meaning.

g9-q4-m13.topic: Using distinct speech sounds in a line
steps: An actor says “Put the ship on the shelf.”
English uses vowel and consonant sounds to distinguish words. Articulation is how we shape those sounds.
Compare ship and sheep. Hold the rest of the line steady so you can hear the different vowel clearly.
Spelling is an unreliable guide to pronunciation by itself.
Listen to the sound and practice it in a line.

g9-q4-m14.topic: Showing meaning through pitch, stress, and pauses
steps: “You finished?” can sound like a check or a surprise.
Pitch is how high or low the voice sounds. Stress gives a syllable or word emphasis. Juncture marks boundaries or pauses. Intonation is the pitch pattern across speech.
Say “You finished?” with rising pitch, then stress you to express surprise about who finished.
A rising arrow only shows pitch direction. It does not by itself show which word is stressed.
Use pitch, stress and pauses to make intention clear.

g10-q1-m1.topic: Finding and confirming key spoken details
steps: An announcement gives a meeting place and time.
Set a listening purpose and capture key details such as who, what, where and when. Confirm any detail that would affect your next step.
If the announcement says “Room 12, Thursday at 3,” write the place, day and time in separate fields.
Filling a gap from memory can turn a guess into a false note.
Listen for the detail you need and verify it.
A safety guide uses bold headings, a diagram and a short table.
A textual aid helps readers find, organize or understand information. Headings name sections, diagrams show relationships and tables support precise comparisons.
A diagram shows where an exit is. A table can tell which exit is nearest to each room.
An image without labels may decorate the guide but leave the route unclear.
Choose the aid for the reading task.
A notice says a workshop starts at 3. An ad calls it “the chance you can’t miss.”
Purpose is what a writer aims to accomplish. Subtext is meaning suggested beneath the words. Identify clues in tone, details and what the writer asks the reader to do.
The notice informs. The ad uses urgency to persuade readers to sign up.
Two texts on the same topic may have different purposes.
Use language and context to justify your reading.

g10-q1-m4.topic: Comparing a passage with its adaptation
steps: In a written scene, Noor thinks the rehearsal room is empty. In the storyboard, she stops when she hears a chair scrape.
An adaptation tells a version of a work in another medium. Compare a matched moment and explain how each medium communicates information through words, sound, framing or performance.
The passage lets us hear Noor’s mistaken assumption as a thought. The storyboard uses sound and her reaction to make the audience discover someone may be there at the same time she does.
Listing changes without explaining their effect leaves the comparison unfinished.
Name the change, cite evidence from both versions and explain its effect.
A printed booklet and a website give different opening hours.
Evaluate a source by its author, evidence, date, purpose and relevance. Format alone tells little about reliability.
Compare the dated library notice with the older booklet and contact the library if the hours still conflict.
A professional-looking website can be out of date.
Check the claim and the source that supports it.

g10-q1-m6.topic: Listening for problems, constraints, and options
steps: A meeting recording describes a flooded walkway and two possible routes.
Analytical listening separates the problem, constraints and evidence from proposed solutions.
An open route without stairs meets the accessibility constraint. Check that it also stays clear of the flooded area.
The first suggestion may overlook a key constraint.
Listen for what a workable solution must satisfy.

g10-q1-m7.topic: Judging texts using the same criteria
steps: Two texts disagree about whether a club should extend its hours.
A reasoned judgment checks a text against clear criteria such as relevance, evidence and the soundness of its conclusion.
A dated sign-in log can support a claim about demand. A recommendation still needs a reason that weighs staff availability.
Agreeing with the conclusion does not make the evidence strong.
Use the same criteria to judge each text.
A speaker gives a clear opening, but the ideas are difficult to follow once the examples begin.

Evaluate fluency, coherence, cohesion, tone, and correctness. Fluency is smooth delivery. Coherence is the overall sense of the ideas. Cohesion is how words and phrases connect them. Tone is the speaker’s attitude. Correctness covers appropriate and accurate language use.
In an original example, a speaker says “first” and “next” while describing two steps in order. Those words create cohesion, while the logical order makes the speech coherent.
Speaking quickly can sound fluent, yet the listener may still struggle if the ideas lack a clear connection.
Check both the way the speaker delivers the message and the way its ideas connect.

g10-q2-m1.topic: Choosing language for research, campaigns, and advocacy
steps: A survey asks a question. A campaign repeats a message. An advocacy statement asks leaders to act.
Research language investigates and reports evidence. Campaign language gains attention. Advocacy argues for a change and calls for action.
A water survey counts leaking taps. “Every drop counts” is a campaign message. A request for a repair budget makes an advocacy case.
A slogan can attract attention without establishing the facts.
Choose language that fits the purpose and evidence.

g10-q2-m2.topic: Connecting claims and reasons with conjunctions
steps: “The plan costs more, but it reaches more students.”
Conjunctions connect ideas and signal relations such as contrast, cause or addition.
But signals contrast. Because could explain why: “We chose the plan because it reaches more students.”
Changing the connector can change the logic of the argument.
Name the relation before choosing a conjunction.

g10-q2-m3.topic: Making a clear opinion or assertion
steps: “I think the library should close later” takes a position.
An opinion states a judgment or preference. An assertion presents a position as a statement that can be examined or supported.
“Extended hours would help students who finish clubs at 4” gives a position that can be supported by attendance records.
A confident assertion still needs a reason and evidence.
Make the position precise enough to discuss and support.
“The plan might work” and “The plan will definitely work” express different certainty.
Modal verbs and modal adverbs qualify claims. Choose the degree of possibility, certainty or obligation that matches the evidence.
A small pilot suggests the change may help. Several consistent trials can justify stronger wording if their conditions match.
Avoid definitely when the evidence shows only a possibility.
Let the evidence set the strength of your wording.

g10-q2-m5.topic: Distinguishing claims of fact, value, and policy
steps: A discussion asks what is true, what is worthwhile and what should be done.
A claim of fact can be checked with evidence. A claim of value judges quality or importance. A claim of policy proposes action.
“The gate closes at 4” is a fact claim. “That is too early” is a value claim. “Keep it open until 5” is a policy claim.
Fact claim describes a type of claim even when it turns out to be false.
Identify what the claim asks the audience to accept.
“Who wants to lose an hour waiting?” invites the audience to consider a point.
A rhetorical question is asked for effect, rather than to collect an answer. It can emphasize an idea or invite reflection.
In a speech, “What could we do with that hour?” draws attention to wasted time. In a survey, the same words could request a genuine response.
A question mark does not tell you the speaker’s purpose.
Read the question in context.
A transport notice pairs a route map with written directions and a spoken update.
A multimodal text combines ways of making meaning, such as words, pictures, sound, movement and spatial layout.
The map shows the route shape, written directions name stops, and spoken audio emphasizes the temporary change.
Repeating the same message in every mode may leave useful details unexplained.
Give each mode a clear job.
A prepared welcome and an unexpected question require different delivery choices.
A prepared speech allows planning and practice. An impromptu speech allows little preparation. Both need a clear point and audience awareness.
For a quick reply, state one point, give one reason, then close. A prepared speech can add examples and rehearsed transitions.
Trying to cover every idea in a short reply can hide the main point.
Organize the speech for the time and audience.

g10-q3-m1.topic: Supporting a claim and answering objections
steps: A proposal asks the school to open a quiet study room.
An argumentative essay supports a claim with reasons and evidence. A counterclaim is an opposing position. A rebuttal answers it fairly.
Claim: Open a room during lunch. Counterclaim: Staff cannot supervise all week. Rebuttal: Pilot two supervised days and measure use.
Mocking the opposing view does not answer its strongest reason.
Support the claim and address the best objection.
A reader wants to know how a rain gauge works.
Informative writing explains a subject clearly. Use definitions, relevant details and an order the reader can follow.
Define rain gauge first, show how water collects, then explain how to read the scale.
Unexplained technical terms can block understanding even when the facts are correct.
Define, explain and organize for the reader.
A poster urges readers to bring a reusable bottle. An article argues for more refill stations.
Persuasion may use appeals to values, feelings or credibility. Argumentation also needs a supported claim and reasoning that addresses objections.
A photo may prompt concern about waste. Refill counts and an explanation of cost help support the policy argument.
An emotional appeal may draw attention without establishing the claim.
Use appeals deliberately and support conclusions with evidence.
“The ending was boring” is an opinion with little support.
A critique evaluates a work using clear criteria and specific evidence. A brief summary gives context for the judgment.
“The ending weakens the mystery because it introduces the key clue only in the final paragraph.” This names a criterion and points to evidence.
Retelling the entire story leaves little room for evaluation.
State a judgment, then show the detail that supports it.

g10-q3-m4.topic: Reading a work through its own elements
steps: A poem repeats an image of a closed window before ending with it open.
A formalist reading examines how the work’s own language, imagery, structure and other elements create meaning.
A closed-to-open window pattern can suggest a shift toward possibility if surrounding words reinforce it.
An unsupported claim about the author’s life does not explain how the poem works.
Explain how textual elements build the interpretation.

g10-q4-m1.topic: Connecting research questions, methods, and samples
steps: A study asks how long students wait in a lunch line.
A research question defines what to find out. A method explains how data are collected. A sample is the group or set observed.
Question: How long is the wait at noon? Method: Record arrival and service times. Sample: Students observed during five lunch periods.
The question and the method serve different purposes.
Use research terms to show how the parts of the study connect.
A study says it will measure reading speed.
A technical definition explains the accepted meaning of a term. An operational definition explains how a particular study observes or measures it.
Reading speed means how quickly someone reads. This study measures it as words read aloud correctly in one minute from a selected passage.
A dictionary meaning alone cannot tell another researcher how to repeat the measurement.
Define what the term means and how the study measures it.

g10-q4-m3.topic: Expanding a definition with useful details
steps: A one-line definition of a budget leaves a reader wondering how it works.
An expanded definition explains a term beyond a single sentence using details such as examples, parts, comparisons or purpose.
A budget is a plan for using money. A school club budget might list expected income, supply costs and the money set aside for later.
Repeating the short definition in different words does little to explain the concept.
Choose details that clarify the term for the reader.
